pass_a_gloss: And this too we must know, that we received the so-called covenants of God on terms, the ones we made toward him when undertaking to live according to Christianity. And among our terms toward God was the whole citizenship according to the gospel, saying: if someone wishes to come behind me, let him deny himself and lift his cross and follow me; for whoever would wish to rescue his soul will destroy it, and whoever would destroy his soul on account of me, this one will rescue it. And often we became more inspired hearing also the saying: for what will a human being be benefited if he makes gain of the whole world but is penalised of his soul; or what will a human being give as a price taken in trade for his soul; for the son of man is about to come in the glory of his father with his angels, and then he will give back to each according to his action. That it is needful to deny oneself and to lift one's own cross and to follow Jesus not Matthew alone, whose wording we placed beside, recorded, but also Luke and Mark. For hear Luke saying: and he was saying toward all: if someone wishes to come behind me, let him deny himself and lift his cross and follow me; for whoever would wish to rescue his soul will destroy it, and whoever would destroy his soul on account of me, this one will rescue it; for what is a human being benefited having made gain of the whole world but having destroyed himself or been penalised. And Mark: and having summoned the crowd with his disciples he said to them: if someone wishes to follow behind me, let him deny himself and lift his cross and follow me; for whoever would wish to rescue his own soul will destroy it, and whoever would destroy it on account of the good news will rescue it; and what will benefit the human being if he makes gain of the whole world and is penalised of his soul; for what will a human being give as a price taken in trade for his soul. Long since therefore we owe it to deny ourselves and to say: I no longer live. And now let it appear whether, having lifted our own cross, we followed Jesus; which has happened if Christ lives in us, if we wish to rescue our soul so that we may take it back better than soul, and destroy it by martyrdom. For if we destroy it on account of Christ, throwing it upon him in the dying on account of him, we will procure for it the true salvation; but if the opposite, we will hear that the one who made gain of the whole perceptible world profits nothing through his own destruction or through having penalised himself. And having once destroyed his own soul or been penalised of it, even if one makes gain of the whole world, he will not be able to give it as a price in trade for the perishing soul. For the soul crafted according to the image of God is of more value than all bodies. One only has been able to give a price in trade for our soul that earlier was perishing, the one who purchased us with his own valuable blood.
pass_b_english: We must also know this: that we received what are called God's covenants on the terms we ourselves agreed with him when we undertook to live as Christians. Among our terms with God was the whole way of life the Gospel sets out, which says: “If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it” (Matthew 16:24-25). And we have often been more deeply inspired on hearing this as well: “For what will a man gain if he wins the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man is about to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to what he has done” (Matthew 16:26-27).

That one must deny oneself, take up one's own cross and follow Jesus is recorded not only by Matthew, whose words we have set out, but also by Luke and Mark. Listen to Luke saying: “He said to all: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it. For what does a man gain if he wins the whole world but loses or forfeits himself?” (Luke 9:23-25). And to Mark: “And calling the crowd to him together with his disciples, he said to them: If anyone wants to follow after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his own soul will lose it; but whoever loses it for the sake of the gospel will save it. And what will it profit a man if he wins the whole world and forfeits his soul? For what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Mark 8:34-37).

We have long been bound, then, to deny ourselves and to say, “It is no longer I who live” (Galatians 2:20). And now let it be made plain whether we have taken up our own cross and followed Jesus. That has come about if “Christ lives in us”: if, wanting to save our soul so as to receive it back as something better than a soul, we also lose it by martyrdom. For if we lose it for Christ's sake, casting it upon him in the death we die for him, we will win true salvation for it; but if we do the opposite, we will hear that the one who has gained the whole world of the senses at the price of his own ruin, or of having forfeited himself, gains nothing. Once someone has lost his own soul or forfeited it, even if he gains the whole world, he will not be able to give that world “in exchange” for the soul that is being lost. For the soul made “after the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) is more precious than all bodies. One alone has been able to give an exchange for our soul, which before was being lost: he who bought us with his own “precious blood” (1 Peter 1:19).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 12); the old English was a digest. The old section 12 carried chapter 13 (Isaiah 43:3-4, Paul caught up to the third heaven), while this chapter's covenant argument and its three Gospel texts on losing the soul sat under old section 11.

Read ὅτε as ὅτι ('that'); ἐμπνουστότεροι γεγόTRUEV as ἐμπνευστότεροι γεγόναμεν ('we have become more inspired'; this clause is in M only, P and Delarue omit it); karrov as ἑαυτόν; „Lo οὐχέτι ἐγώ as ζῶ οὐκέτι ἐγώ; el „Gi“ ἐν ἡμῖν as εἰ ζῇ ἐν ἡμῖν; φυχῆς as ψυχῆς; dednu μιουργημένη as δεδημιουργημένη.
'Soul' throughout, including in the Gospel quotations, because Origen's argument turns on it: receiving the soul back 'better than a soul' and the soul made after God's image.

choices.issue: Construal of εἰ θέλομεν ... ἵνα ... ἀπολάβωμεν ..., καὶ μαρτυρίῳ ἀπολέσωμεν
choices.choice: Taken as one condition: if, wanting to save our soul so as to receive it back better, we also lose it by martyrdom.
αὐτόν refers to the world just gained: 'give that world in exchange'.
Koetschau prints 'more precious than all bodies' (M); P and Delarue omit 'bodies'. English follows Koetschau.
